narrative:
Based on the available information, there is a 68% chance that you will leave your job in the near future, and that is why the promotion is being denied. In short, the model sees signs that you are not likely to stay long enough to make the investment in promoting you worthwhile.

The strongest factor working in your favor is your training record. Attending more than seven programs in the last three years is unusual—only about one in five loyal employees have that many—and it strongly suggests you are engaged and growing within the organization. This pushes the prediction toward staying, which is good.

However, two other signals override that positive impression. You have received other job opportunities while working here, which is relatively rare among employees who stay (only about 23% of them do). This tells the model that you are actively attractive to other employers and may be tempted to leave. At the same time, your total experience of 11 years or more is also uncommon among employees who remain—only about 15% of stayers have that much experience. Experienced professionals like you often move on for better roles, and the model weighs that heavily.

Taken together, these factors say that while you are deeply trained, your outside options and long career history make turnover a real risk. To change this picture, consider how you can demonstrate commitment—whether by discussing your long-term plans with leadership or seeking clarity on growth paths within the organization. That would help reassure decision-makers that you see your future here.
